'''Ian Colin Percival''' (born 27 July 1931)<ref name="WW">{{Who's Who | title = PERCIVAL, Prof. Ian Colin | id = U30552 | volume = 2026 | edition = online}}</ref>  is a British theoretical physicist. He is the Emeritus Professor of the School of Physics and Astronomy<ref>{{citation|title=Home Page|url=http://ph.qmul.ac.uk/directory/i.c.percival|access-date=5 June 2014|archive-date=16 April 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180416200900/http://ph.qmul.ac.uk/directory/i.c.percival|url-status=dead}}</ref> at [[Queen Mary University of London|Queen Mary University]], [[University of London]]. 

==Education==
Percival was educated at [[Ealing County Grammar School]] and [[University College London]], where he took his BSc and PhD.<ref name="WW"/>

==Career==
He is one among the pioneers of [[quantum chaos]] and he is well known for his suggestion in the 1970s about the existence of a different type of spectra of quantum-mechanical systems due to classical chaos.<ref>Percival ''Regular and irregular spectra'', J. Phys. B, volume 6, 1973, L 229–232</ref> Numerical explorations performed by other researchers clearly confirmed this idea later. In 1987, with Franco Vivaldi, he used the algebraic number theory of quadratic number fields to count the periodic orbits in generalized Arnold-Sinai [[Arnold's cat map|cat maps]].<ref>Percival, Vivaldi ''Arithmetical properties of strongly chaotic motion'', Physica D, volume 25, 1987, p. 105</ref> Later on, he worked on the basics of quantum mechanics and the measurement process. Together with Walter Strunz, he suggested the properties of the quantum foam at the Planck scale (similar to the movement of particles due to Brownian motion) in the wave function of an atom-beam interference.<ref>Percival, Strunz ''Detection of space-time fluctuations by a model matter interferometer'', Proc. Roy. Soc., A, 453, 1997, pp. 431–446. Percival ''Atom interferometry, spacetime and reality'', Physics World, März 1997</ref>

==Awards==
In 1985 he was awarded the [[Naylor Prize]]. In 1999 he was awarded the [[Dirac Medal (IOP)|Paul Dirac Medal and Prize]] by the [[Institute of Physics]].
He is a Fellow of the [[Royal Society]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fellow Detail Page {{!}} Royal Society |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/12079/ |access-date=2024-02-22 |website=royalsociety.org}}</ref>

==Books and articles==
*Together with Derek Richards: ''Introduction to Dynamics'', Cambridge University Press 1982
*"Chaos: A Science for the Real World", in Nina Hall (editor), ''The New Scientist Guide to Chaos'', Penguin 1992 (also ''New Scientist'', 21 October 1989)
*''Quantum State Diffusion'', Cambridge University Press 1998
*Together with Nicolas Gisin, "The Quantum-State Diffusion Model applied to Open Systems", ''Journal of Physics A'', volume 25, 1992, pp.&nbsp;5677–91
*Published with P. Cvitanović, A. Wirzba: ''Quantum Chaos–Quantum Measurement'', Kluwer 1992 (in which by Percival: "Quantum Records")
*Published with [[Michael Berry (physicist)|Michael Berry]], Nigel Oscar Weiss: ''Dynamical Chaos'', Royal Society London 1987, Princeton University Press 1989 (Royal Society Discussion Meeting 4–5 February 1987)
*"Chaos in Hamiltonian Systems", ''Proc. Roy. Soc., A'', volume 413, 1987, pp.&nbsp;131–143
*"Integrable and nonintegrable Hamiltonian systems'" in'''Non-linear dynamics aspects of particle accelerators'', Lecture Notes in Physics, volume 247, 1986, pp.&nbsp;12–36
